The Right to Be Forgotten and Freedom of the Press in Italy: Where the Line Falls

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

In Italy the right to be forgotten does not override freedom of the press; the two are balanced case by case. An article that was lawful when published can later have to be deindexed, updated or anonymised once its public interest has faded, while news that still serves the public, or concerns a person with an ongoing public role, stays fully accessible.

Why the two rights collide

The conflict arises because both rights have constitutional weight. Freedom of the press rests on art. 21 of the Italian Constitution and on the journalist's right to report facts of public interest (diritto di cronaca); the right to be forgotten (diritto all'oblio) derives from personal identity and data protection, codified in art. 17 GDPR.

European law itself anticipates the tension. Art. 17(3)(a) GDPR excludes erasure where processing is necessary for exercising freedom of expression and information, and art. 85 obliges Member States to reconcile data protection with journalism. Italy did so through the Codice Privacy and the professional rules on processing personal data in journalism, which require relevance, essentiality of information and particular care with minors, health data and criminal matters. The question in every dispute about the right to be forgotten vs freedom of the press is therefore not which right wins in the abstract, but whether keeping a specific piece of information prominently accessible is still justified today.

The balancing test: what decides the outcome

Courts and the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali look at a recurring set of criteria, and a request succeeds only when most of them point the same way. No single factor, including the age of an article, is decisive on its own.

  • The current public interest in the facts, not the interest they had when first reported.
  • The time elapsed, measured against the seriousness and nature of the events.
  • The role the person plays in public life now, not only at the time of publication.
  • Whether the information is accurate, complete and updated, for example after an acquittal.
  • The type of data involved, with stronger protection for health, sexual life and criminal records.

Public interest has an expiry date

News about a fraud investigation into a Milan entrepreneur is plainly of public interest when it happens. Fifteen years later, after a dismissal and no further involvement in public affairs, the same article mainly serves to define a private person by an old episode. Italian case law treats this shift as central: the informational value of a fact is not permanent and must be reassessed when the article keeps surfacing on a name search.

A public role keeps information relevant

Politicians, senior public officials, directors of listed companies and other people who still exercise influence face a much higher threshold. Their past conduct may remain relevant for judging current decisions, so time alone rarely suffices. Someone who has left public life, however, gradually regains the protection of a private individual.

How the Italian Supreme Court approaches the conflict

Right to be forgotten case law in Italy, shaped mainly by the Corte di Cassazione, distinguishes between three different situations, each with its own standard. Treating them separately is the key to understanding why some requests succeed and others fail.

The first situation is the republication of old news. When a newspaper brings back a dated story about a private person, the Court has required a renewed and current public interest; without it, reviving the episode can be unlawful even if the original reporting was correct. A ruling of the Joint Sections (Sezioni Unite) in 2019 emphasised this point for retrospective articles: historical reconstruction is legitimate, but naming a private individual must itself be justified by present relevance.

The second concerns online archives. The Cassazione has recognised that a publisher keeping articles accessible must ensure they are not misleading, which can mean adding an update or a note about later developments rather than deleting the piece. The third is deindexing: removing the link between a person's name and the article in search engines, while the article stays in the archive. This follows the logic of the Court of Justice of the EU in Google Spain (C-131/12) and is generally seen as the least invasive remedy, since it preserves the historical record and limits only its easy discoverability.

Journalism and online archives: which remedy fits

For right to be forgotten and journalism, the realistic goal is rarely deletion. The outcome usually falls into one of three remedies, chosen according to how intrusive the remaining exposure is.

RemedyWhat changesTypical situation
DeindexingArticle stays online, but no longer appears for searches of the nameOld, accurate news about a private person with no current public role
Update or contextualisationA note or new paragraph reports later developmentsInvestigation reported, acquittal or dismissal never mentioned
AnonymisationName or identifying details replaced with initialsMinors, victims, marginal figures in a story, sensitive data

Deindexing is handled through Google's request form and, if refused, through a complaint to the Garante or a court. Updates and anonymisation depend on the publisher, who can be approached directly with a reasoned request citing the professional rules for journalists. For people acquitted or whose case was dismissed, the Riforma Cartabia added a specific court-ordered route under art. 64-ter of the implementing provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The broader limits of what can disappear from search are covered in our article on what the right to be forgotten can really remove from Google.

When freedom of the press prevails

The press wins the balance whenever the information still contributes to a debate of general interest. This is not a technicality: requests that ignore it are rejected, and pursuing them can draw fresh attention to the article.

Typical examples include convictions for serious crimes that remain recent relative to their gravity, conduct connected to a public office the person still holds or seeks, business activities affecting consumers or investors where the individual is still active in the same sector, and matters of historical or institutional significance. Corrections of fact are a different issue: an inaccurate article calls for a correction under the press law (rettifica) or, in certain cases, a defamation claim, rather than an argument about the passage of time.

The right to be forgotten protects people from being permanently defined by information that no longer serves the public. It does not protect anyone from information the public still has a legitimate reason to know.

Building a request that respects the balance

A successful request openly addresses the journalistic value of the content and explains why that value has faded, rather than simply stating that the article is harmful. Reviewers at Google, the Garante and Italian judges all respond to this structure.

  1. Identify every URL and the exact search queries on which each appears.
  2. Reconstruct what happened after publication, with documents such as judgments, dismissal orders or company records.
  3. Show the current absence of a public role and the concrete harm, for example in employment or business relationships.
  4. Choose the least intrusive remedy that solves the problem, starting with deindexing or updating.
  5. Escalate to the Garante or a court only with a complete file, since a weak first attempt becomes part of the record.
